prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, enabling measurement of time and frequency at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: Eight of eight members ranked the optical lattice clock, and all eight proposed the same two names, Katori and Ye. That agreement on attribution is rare on this list and counts for something, although I do not equate it with merit. On the science, the magic-wavelength idea removes the light shift of the trapping field, so that thousands of neutral atoms can be held and interrogated at once without perturbing the clock transition. This gives both accuracy and stability at the 10^-18 level, and it has led to new measurements: gravitational redshift across millimetres, bounds on drifts of constants and on dark-matter couplings, and many-body effects such as spin-exchange and SU(N) physics inside the clock itself. These are quantum-mechanical systems that we can now control and read out with extraordinary resolution, which is the kind of progress in precision I value. It has been reproduced and improved by many laboratories (JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE, NPL and others) for about twenty years, and the interpretation is not disputed. It is a different step from the 2005 prize for the comb and the 2012 prize for individual-ion control, because it works with neutral atoms in a lattice and it created the regime of many-atom clocks.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is that metrology was recognised in 2005 (Hall and Haensch) and in 2012 (Wineland), so a third prize in this area may look like a refinement of established tools rather than a new discovery. The redefinition of the second has not yet occurred, so the largest consequence is still pending, and some will say the work is a technique and not a finding about nature. There is also a real attribution question: Katori's proposal and Ye's accuracy demonstrations are not the whole story, and the ion-clock groups (for example Al+ clocks) are in a competing line that remains a strong rival at similar uncertainty. I also note my own bias: as an atomic theorist, I find this area natural and may undervalue arguments from other fields.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the IceCube detection of a diffuse astrophysical neutrino flux first, as a genuine clue from nature and the opening of a new window on the extreme universe, with the concern that three names do not capture the collaboration and predecessors such as AMANDA and Baikal.
responses.response: I agree that this is the most striking discovery of the observational kind on the list, and I ranked it sixth only because I defer to him and Pearce on astrophysics. My hesitation is the one he states himself. The result rests on a collaboration of several hundred people, the predecessor experiments are not trivial, and source identification beyond TXS 0506+056 and NGC 1068 is still thin and not yet independently confirmed. The lattice clock does not have that problem: two people, clear priority for the key idea, and many independent confirmations. If the committee finds the neutrino attribution can be settled, I would see B007 as a serious competitor and have placed it as an alternative. I would not call the lattice clock incremental, as he fears, because the neutral-atom lattice made a different regime available.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first, since a continuum-model prediction of flat bands was followed by decisive experiments and opened a field, and he values the quantitative link between model and measurement.
responses.response: I share his admiration for the Bistritzer-MacDonald model; it is a simple picture that predicted something non-obvious, and that is what I like in a theory. My reservation is about maturity and fairness rather than merit. The pairing mechanism of the superconductivity is still unsettled, sample-to-sample variability remains, and the 2018 discovery involved junior researchers (Cao and others) who are outside the credited three. That makes the prize harder to defend today than in a few years. The lattice clock is also a case where theory and experiment agree quantitatively, with a longer track record of independent reproduction. I would still support B006 as my alternative if the committee prefers condensed matter, but I would want the attribution question settled first.

responses.point: Mehlig also places twisted bilayer graphene first, as a minimal mechanism that is understood and not only observed, while ranking the lattice clock fourth.
responses.response: His point about explanation rather than observation is fair, and I accept that the clock is largely a measurement achievement and not a new mechanism. Yet the clock is also understood at a very deep level; the systematic shifts are modelled and checked against each other across laboratories, and that is the standard by which I judge precision work. I would also push back on a ranking that implies the clock is less fundamental: what it tests, gravitational redshift at millimetre scale and constancy of constants, is fundamental. I agree with him that MacDonald with Jarillo-Herrero is the natural pairing, and that three names for B006 leaves an uncomfortable theory-credit question.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the lattice clock first and atom interferometry second, arguing that progress here is limited by how precisely one can measure and that atom interferometers are a new class of instrument.
responses.response: I agree with him on the lattice clock and on the minor allocation issue between Katori and Ye. I am more cautious about atom interferometry than my own third place suggests. The priority story is tangled (Chu, Borde, Helmcke and Mlynek, Pritchard, Kasevich), and a clean three-name assignment is hard; part of the atom-optics toolkit was also implicitly covered in 1997 and 2001. For me that is a reason to keep the clock first and treat interferometry as a candidate for a later year, not a reason to bundle the two. Two parts with five names are not allowed in any case.

uncertainties: Whether the committee judges the lattice clock sufficiently distinct from the 2005 and 2012 metrology prizes.
The exact weighting of Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and early Sr clock against Ye's accuracy and stability records, and whether other groups merit mention in the citation text.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second should be awaited, and how much the competing ion-clock line should weigh.
The attribution and maturity issues for B006 and B007 that I have raised for colleagues; I rely on memory for priority details.
statement.conflict_note: I am a long-time close collaborator of Anne L'Huillier (2023 laureate) and have co-authored with the Lund and Ursula Keller (ETH) attosecond groups, but my profile shows no connection to Katori, Ye or their groups, so no specific conflict is apparent for B015. Atomic physics is my own field, which is a bias to declare, not a recusal ground. I have no apparent connection to the candidates in B006 or B007.
